articles.title: Google Rewrites Meta Descriptions Often: What SMBs Should Do to Protect CTR
articles.excerpt: Google does not reliably show the meta description that a business writes for its pages. Analysis cited by Search Engine Land found that about 70% of tracked queries displayed a Google-written descrip…
articles.body: Google does not reliably show the meta description that a business writes for its pages. Analysis cited by Search Engine Land found that about 70% of tracked queries displayed a Google-written description , and a single page could show several snippet variations over a month. For SMBs, the implication is not that meta descriptions are obsolete. It is that search-result messaging now depends on both the description tag and the page content Google may use instead. The practical goal is to treat the meta description as a CTR asset rather than a ranking lever . A clear, relevant description can still encourage a qualified searcher to click.

articles.title: 41 Years, the Most Inventive Sci-Fi Thriller of the '80s Is Officially Free to Watch on Streaming
articles.excerpt: This cult classic remains one of the most inventive zombie movies ever made.
articles.body: Zombies are some of the most difficult creatures to innovate. Over nearly a century of cinematic history , these monsters have typically been frightening but simple; they eat brains and they decompose. The zombie genre itself is defined by its clear parameters, usually depicting the rise of the undead, a group of survivors, and a collapsing society. While the storytelling has evolved to explore different societal concerns, the zombie genre remains challenging to add wrinkles to. Some of the biggest breakthroughs in the genre come from redefining the zombie itself: 28 Days Later made them fast and angry (and technically not undead at all), while The Last of Us fused real science and speculative sci-fi to imagine a connected network of fungus-infected zombies.
articles.author: Maria Loreto

articles.title: Per-user two-factor auth in CakePHP with CakeDC/Users (opt-in, one method)
articles.excerpt: CakeDC/Users gives you TOTP two-factor authentication almost for free: flip one config key and every login grows a "enter your 6-digit code" step. The catch is that word every. The built-in flow is al…
articles.body: CakeDC/Users gives you TOTP two-factor authentication almost for free: flip one config key and every login grows a "enter your 6-digit code" step. The catch is that word every . The built-in flow is all-or-nothing — turn it on and all your users are forced through the OTP challenge on their next login, whether they ever set up an authenticator app or not. Lock yourself out on a fresh install and you'll find out fast. What most apps actually want is the model you see everywhere else: 2FA is off by default , and each user opts in from their own account settings. This post shows how to get there with a surprisingly small change — one overridden method — plus a self-service enrolment screen and one QR-code gotcha that will bite you on modern dependencies.

articles.title: I built an open cross-reference dataset for 217 global steel grades so engineers stop guessing "is that equivalent?"
articles.excerpt: __ ASTM A36 while your supplier quotes S275JR, you know the moment of dread: are these actually equivalent, or am I about to spec the wrong material into a load-bearing structure? Most engineers resol…
articles.body: __ If you've ever received a spec that says ASTM A36 while your supplier quotes S275JR , you know the moment of dread: are these actually equivalent, or am I about to spec the wrong material into a load-bearing structure? Most engineers resolve this with a bookmark tab open to five different standards lookup sites, a PDF from 2009, and a prayer. It's slow, error-prone, and the "winner" is usually whichever site ranks first — not whichever grade is chemically and mechanically right for the job. I got tired of it, so I built a dataset. What I actually built A cross-reference database of 217 steel and alloy grades , each normalized against five standards systems: ASTM, EN (European Norm), JIS, GB (Chinese), and IS (Indian) .

articles.title: Pluto losing its planet status may be the best thing that ever happened to solar system diversity
articles.excerpt: Unpopular opinion time, Pluto being reclassified as a dwarf planet was a great thing for our understanding of the solar system and for the former planet, too.
articles.body: Unpopular opinion time, but someone has to say it: I think Pluto being reclassified as a dwarf planet was a great thing for our understanding of the solar system and for the former planet itself. Let me try to convince you, too. First, a little background. The Pluto planet controversy began exactly 20 years ago on Aug. 24, 2006, when the International Astronomical Union (IAU) reclassified the solar system's (former) ninth planet as a dwarf planet. The reason for the change was the result of the discovery of worlds similar to Pluto in the Kuiper Belt , the ring of icy bodies and debris extending out beyond the orbit of Neptune. It suddenly became necessary to determine if these bodies are planets or whether the definition of what a planet is needs to be reshaped.

articles.body: Amiable sci-fi author Andy Weir, the New York Times bestselling author of " The Martian ," " Artemis ," and " Project Hail Mary ", is embarking on an entirely new imaginative odyssey later this year. It's not exactly another sci-fi book, though; It's an audiobook, and Weir is foregoing sole authorship of the project and instead co-shepherding this captivating space opera drama for the folks at Audible. Arriving on Nov. 5, 2026, "Exoplanet" is an ambitious celestial thriller written by comic book veteran and acclaimed author Benjamin Percy ("Red Moon"), executive produced by Weir, and showcasing a stellar vocal cast that includes Anthony Mackie, the Oscar-winning Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

articles.body: The rumors are true. SpaceX plans to retire its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket once the company's giant next-generation Starship begins regular operational flights. SpaceX launched the Falcon 9 for the first time in 2010, and the rocket soon chiselled itself a place in spaceflight history. The Falcon 9 has lifted off nearly 700 times to date, and it's the first orbital rocket ever to land and refly its first-stage booster. Russia's Soyuz rocket , which has been in operation since 1957, is the only launch vehicle with more missions under its belt, but the Falcon 9 is on track to pass it next year.
